title: How to organize image references on a floating board
description: Build a small image reference board for a design task: choose useful images, keep sources, compare details and know when to use a dedicated mood board tool.
alt: FloatBoard in dark mode displaying four landscape image references in a two-column grid
caption: A four-image board keeps a small set of references visible together. This screenshot shows the FloatBoard image layout; the workflow below is an illustrative example.
intro: An image reference board is useful when you need to compare a few visual ideas while working in another app. The hard part is choosing what belongs on it. A folder of fifty pictures can be a collection; a useful reference board should help you make a specific decision.

sections.title: Start with a design question, not a pile of pictures
sections.html:
Before adding images, write one sentence describing the decision you need to make. For example: ‘Choose a warm evening palette with a quiet, open composition.’ This gives every image a job. One might show the light, another the amount of empty space, and another the contrast between foreground and background.

The screenshot above contains four different landscapes. For this example, the coastal sunset can be a reference for warm light, the palm scene for reflections, the mountain scene for silhouette, and the darker landscape for contrast. Those are observations to compare, not four instructions to reproduce in one design.

If you cannot explain why an image is on your board, leave it in your source folder for now. A small board that answers one question is easier to use than a larger board whose images compete for attention.

sections.title: Build a working set you can see beside your app
sections.html:
1. Keep the originals. Save your source files in a project folder. Treat the board as a working reference, not your only archive.
  2. Choose a few distinct references. Avoid filling the board with almost identical images. Pick the examples that reveal different aspects of your question.
  3. Add the images to FloatBoard. Use the image workflow available in your installed version. The image panel keeps the references together, as shown in the screenshot.
  4. Place the window beside your canvas. Use the pin / always-on-top control so the board remains visible when you return to the design app. Leave enough space for the actual work.
  5. Check readability. If important details are too small, work with fewer references or use a larger view. A tiny thumbnail is suitable for overall composition, but not fine typography or texture.

FloatBoard’s free plan has image limits. Check the current plan details before planning a larger collection; this workflow does not require filling every available slot.

sections.title: Record what each reference teaches you
sections.html:
Images alone do not preserve the reasoning behind a design. Keep a short note in your project document with three fields: source, detail to study, and decision. For example: ‘Coastal sunset — warm highlights against a darker foreground — try a warm accent on a neutral background.’

Save the source URL and any usage or licensing information with the original. Collecting an image for reference does not give you permission to publish it. When it is time to deliver the project, choose assets you own or have permission to use.

After each design pass, write down which reference helped. If two images now serve the same purpose, keep the clearer one on the working board. This makes the next pass a focused comparison instead of another round of browsing.

sections.title: Fix the common problems before adding more images
sections.html:
The board covers your work: move or resize it rather than squeezing your canvas into the remaining space. On a small screen, it can be more useful to compare two images at a time.

You keep collecting but do not decide: return to the opening question. Choose one visual direction, make a small draft, and compare that draft against your references. The board supports a decision; it does not make one.

You need precise color values: return to the original asset and your design app’s color tools. A scaled screenshot or thumbnail should not be treated as an authoritative color measurement.

sections.title: When a floating board is the right tool
sections.html:
A floating image board fits a short, individual task with a small set of visual references. For an extensive asset library, keep folders and a catalog. For shared comments, layout planning or a presentation-ready mood board, use a tool built for those tasks. Do not assume that a visible grid provides collaboration or asset management.

If you also need written instructions beside your images, see the reference-notes workflow. For a small visual task, download FloatBoard, choose one question and build a board that helps you answer it.

title: Keep code snippets and screenshots together while debugging
description: Use a temporary reference board for a UI debugging task. Keep a screenshot, relevant code and expected behavior together without losing the original sources.
alt: FloatBoard with four image thumbnails on the left and a text card containing HTML markup on the right
caption: FloatBoard can show image references and text side by side. The HTML in this screenshot is a reference snippet, not an executable code editor.
intro: A UI bug often sends you between an editor, a browser and a screenshot. A temporary board can keep the few details you are comparing in view. The useful unit is one debugging question: one visual symptom, one relevant snippet and one statement of what should happen.

sections.title: Capture the context that a copied snippet loses
sections.html:
A fragment such as an opening HTML tag tells you little when separated from its file. Alongside a snippet, record the file path, the component name and what you were checking. If the code comes from documentation, keep the documentation URL and the library version relevant to your project.

For a screenshot, note the viewport size, the action that produced the problem and the expected result. A screenshot of a clipped button is more actionable when the accompanying note says it happens after opening the menu at a narrow viewport.

Keep private credentials, access tokens and customer information out of a reference board. Copy only the minimum code and visual context needed to investigate the issue.

sections.title: Set up a board for one layout bug
sections.html:
1. Reproduce the symptom. Use your normal browser or app testing workflow and capture the affected area. Keep the original screenshot in the project’s issue or working folder.
  2. Find the smallest relevant snippet. Copy the markup or styling you need to compare. Include enough surrounding context to identify it, but avoid copying an entire file.
  3. Add the references to FloatBoard. Use the text and image panels to keep the snippet and screenshot available together. The supplied screenshot demonstrates this side-by-side layout.
  4. Write an expected result. For example: ‘The image grid should stay within the panel at 390 pixels wide.’ Put this beside your working notes rather than relying on memory.
  5. Pin the board and return to your editor. Position it where it does not cover the lines you are changing. Use it for reference while the editor and browser remain the tools that modify and test the code.

sections.title: Example: a reference note for a clipped image grid
sections.html:
Suppose image cards extend beyond their container. Instead of collecting unrelated examples, make a short note with the following structure:

Question: Why does the image grid overflow?
File: styles/gallery.css
Reproduce: open gallery at a 390px viewport
Expected: cards fit without horizontal scrolling
Reference: screenshot of the overflowing panel
Next check: grid columns, item min-width, image sizing

This is an illustrative debugging checklist, not a diagnosis of FloatBoard. Its purpose is to keep the question and evidence together. Inspect the actual elements in your browser, change one relevant constraint, then repeat the same reproduction steps. Update the note with what changed rather than adding a second unexplained snippet.

A reference board does not run code, validate HTML or replace developer tools. The result is only confirmed when your application behaves correctly in the relevant test environment.

sections.title: Use clipboard history for retrieval, the board for comparison
sections.html:
Clipboard history is useful when you need to retrieve something you copied earlier. A visible reference board solves a different problem: keeping selected material in sight while you work. Do not assume that a clipboard manager automatically gives a copied fragment the context of a documented snippet.

When you retrieve an older clip, compare it with the current source file before reusing it. A copied snippet is a snapshot; later changes in the repository do not automatically update that text. For the broader product workflow, read the clipboard manager guide.

sections.title: Finish with a reproducible record
sections.html:
Once the issue is fixed, put the reproduction steps, final change and relevant screenshot in the project’s normal record, such as an issue or commit description. Keep long-lived snippets in a repository or documentation tool where they can be reviewed and maintained.

Then clear out references that no longer support the task. Avoid turning the board into an unlabelled backlog of old errors. If you need to compare many files, use the editor’s split view; if you need a shared review, use your team’s review tools.

Get FloatBoard for your operating system to try this with a small task. Check the free-plan limits first, and choose only the text and images needed to answer your current debugging question.

title: How to keep reference notes visible while writing
description: Set up always-on-top reference notes beside a draft. Keep source links, quotations and image reminders separate from your own wording with a practical writing workflow.
alt: FloatBoard showing text reference cards on the left and six image thumbnails on the right
caption: Text and image references can share a FloatBoard window. The screenshot shows the layout; the writing example below uses its own illustrative notes.
intro: When a draft depends on a few source details, repeatedly reopening the source can interrupt the sentence you are writing. A small set of always-on-top notes can keep those details beside your document. The key is to separate evidence from your own ideas and leave enough screen space to write comfortably.

sections.title: Choose notes for the next section of your draft
sections.html:
Start with the paragraph or section you are about to write, not the whole research project. Pick the information you expect to consult repeatedly: a short quotation, a source link, a question the paragraph must answer, or an image you need to describe.

Keep the original material in its normal location. A floating note is a working reference, not a substitute for the source document. If a fact needs a date, unit or qualification to remain accurate, include that context rather than copying only the attractive sentence.

For an image reference, write down what you are looking at and where it came from. This matters especially when a thumbnail resembles several other files in the project.

sections.title: Place the notes beside your writing window
sections.html:
1. Open the draft first. Choose a comfortable document width and text size. The reference board should fit around your writing, not force the draft into a narrow strip.
  2. Add a short working note to FloatBoard. Label a quotation as a quotation and include its source. Put your own interpretation in a separate labelled block.
  3. Add a visual reference only if it helps. The screenshot shows text and images in separate panels. You do not need to fill both panels for a text-only task.
  4. Enable always-on-top. Use the pin control and place the board beside the draft. Switch back to your writing app to check that the reference remains visible.
  5. Write a paragraph before adding more. If you repeatedly need information that is missing, add that detail. If a note is distracting, remove it from the current working set.

On a small screen, side-by-side windows may leave too little room. Try a shorter note or your operating system’s window arrangement tools. A floating window is useful only when it makes the reference easier to read.

sections.title: Example: prepare a product-description draft
sections.html:
Imagine writing a short description of a desktop notes app. Your working note could look like this:

Section: What the app helps you do
Source: official feature page + date checked
Confirmed detail: notes stay visible above other windows
My explanation: keep a short reference beside a draft
Check before publishing: supported systems and plan limits

This is a template, not a claim that every notes app provides those features. Replace the details with the product you have actually checked. For FloatBoard, the floating notes overview, download page and pricing page provide the product context.

The distinction between ‘confirmed detail’ and ‘my explanation’ helps prevent a useful interpretation from becoming an unsupported product claim. Before publishing, return to the source and verify the wording and any numbers.

sections.title: Keep quotations, sources and your own wording distinct
sections.html:
Use quotation marks for copied wording and keep a link or document reference with it. When you paraphrase, check that your sentence preserves the meaning, not just the topic. A visible note can make source checking easier, but it does not perform that check for you.

Do not use the board as an excuse to copy someone else’s text into a finished article without attribution or permission where required. If you are working with sensitive research or private correspondence, use only the information appropriate for that workspace and avoid including it in screenshots you share.

For a longer research project, use a reference manager or organized source document. Those tools are better suited to bibliographies and large collections; a floating board is for the small subset needed right now.

sections.title: Review the draft, then refresh the working set
sections.html:
At the end of the section, check each factual statement against its original source. Move useful long-term notes into your project document. Then replace the working references with the material needed for the next section.

If you mostly need to recover previously copied text, read the clipboard history guide. If you are comparing visual ideas instead of writing prose, the image reference board workflow explains how to keep that task focused.

You can try this workflow with one window and a small number of notes. FloatBoard’s free plan includes 5 texts and 5 images per day; check the pricing page for current details rather than building a workflow around an assumed unlimited plan.
